Abo.note: Everything here is an Abo, and every Abo has a notice period

Abstimmung.note: Four times a year an envelope comes and you tick yes or no

Alu.note: Goes back to the shop, like PET

Apotheke.note: The first stop for small things. They advise, and send you on when it is more

Artikel.note: der, die or das. Learn it welded to the noun or you will be Nuno

Ausweis.note: Swiss. Also the driving licence, where Germany says Führerschein

Automat.note: Weak noun: den Automaten, dem Automaten

Bon.note: Swiss, from the French. Germany says Kassenbon or Quittung

Brockenhaus.note: Swiss. Furnishing from one is normal, not poor

Brunnen.note: Public ones run drinking water unless a sign says otherwise

Crème.note: Short for Kaffee crème, the standard Swiss coffee. You order einen Crème

Fasnacht.note: Luzern starts at five in the morning and runs six days

Franchise.note: What you pay yourself before the insurer starts. A high one means a low premium

Föhn.note: Warm dry wind off the Alps. Blamed for headaches and bad moods

Gebührensack.note: You pay for collection through the price of the bag. The wrong bag is not taken

Gemeinde.note: The local authority. Everything else follows from registering with it

Gleis.note: The numbered track a train leaves from

Grüezi.note: The Swiss greeting. Said to strangers, and not saying it is noticed

Guggenmusik.note: They practise all year in order to play deliberately out of tune

Hausordnung.note: Hangs in every Swiss building and everybody keeps to it

Hauswart.note: Not a landlord and not a servant. You report a problem to him

Herr.note: Herrn in every case but the nominative

Hoi.note: Only to somebody you would du. Hoi zäme to more than one

Krankenkasse.note: Compulsory, private, and yours to choose within three months

Leute.note: Plural only. There is no singular

Mahnung.note: What arrives if you miss the Frist. It costs

Occasion.note: Swiss, from the French. A used car or bike is an Occasion

Post.note: Always yellow, as are its vans and buses

Punkt.note: Punkt acht means eight o’clock sharp

Rappen.note: One hundredth of a franc. Nothing below five

Recht.note: Recht haben is to be right

Ruhezeit.note: Ten at night to seven, midday to one, and all of Sunday

Sali.note: From the French salut. Informal, and strongest around Zurich, Basel and the centre

Schale.en: coffee with a lot of milk
Schale.note: Swiss. A Crème is the ordinary one, a Schale is the milky one

Schiff.note: On the lakes it runs to a timetable, like a bus

Schweiz.note: Always with the article: die Schweiz

See.note: Der See is a lake. Die See is the sea

Sie.note: Always capitalised. You start here with everybody and wait to be offered du

Sonntag.note: Shops shut. The station is the exception

Sonntagabend.note: Sonntag + Abend. German glues words together and you can read them apart

Stock.note: The first Stock is one ABOVE the ground floor, which is the Erdgeschoss

Strasse.note: Never with an eszett in Switzerland

Tschüss.note: Heard, mostly from younger people. Ade is the Luzern word

Ursache.note: Keine Ursache means: no trouble at all

Wein.note: Migros has never sold it. Coop does

Wiedersehen.note: Only really used in auf Wiedersehen. Here people say Ade

Zug.note: Also a town, and the train stops there

dabei.note: Ich habe es dabei means I have it on me

danke.note: Correct, but merci is heard more often here

doch.note: A particle. It contradicts, softens or insists depending on the sentence

dran.note: Ich bin dran means it is my turn

fressen.note: Used of animals, never of people

gar.note: Almost always with nicht: gar nicht means not at all

gefallen.note: Das gefällt mir is how you say I like it

geschehen.note: Gern geschehen is you are welcome

gewöhnen.note: Always with sich an: ich gewöhne mich an den Winter

gleichfalls.note: Hands any good wish straight back. Schönen Abend — merci, gleichfalls

kennen.en: to know a person or place

los.note: Ich gehe los means I set off

merci.note: Everyday German in Switzerland, not a French word borrowed for the occasion

mitenand.note: Grüezi mitenand is what you say to two or more people

möchten.note: The polite want. Ich möchte einen Kaffee

stimmen.note: Das stimmt means that is true

tiptop.note: The everyday answer to Wie gaht’s. Spelled tiptop here, not tipptopp

weh.note: Only really in weh tun, to hurt

patterns.title: Grüezi — the word you cannot skip
patterns.text:
You greet BEFORE anything else. Walking into a shop and saying what you want, with no Grüezi in front of it, is what badly brought up people do.

• **Grüezi** to one person you do not know
• **Grüezi mitenand** to two or more
• **Hoi** or **Sali** to a friend, never to a stranger
• **Ade** on the way out

And you greet people you will never speak to again. The lift, the waiting room, a narrow pavement. Not saying it is noticed, and nobody will ever mention it.

**merci** is ordinary German here, not a French word borrowed for the occasion. Danke is correct and you will hear it far less.

patterns.title: Der, die, das — three words for "the"
patterns.text:
Every German noun carries a gender, and it is not about the thing.

• **der** Mann, **der** Zug, **der** See, **der** Berg
• **die** Frau, **die** Strasse, **die** Uhr, **die** Nacht
• **das** Haus, **das** Wasser, **das** Brot, **das** Kind

Das Mädchen is neuter. There is no logic to find, so do not look for one.

**Learn the article welded to the word.** Not "Zug, masculine" but "der Zug", one lump, the way you learned your own first words. Every entry in this course states it, and it costs nothing now and everything later.

patterns.title: The verb comes second. Always second.
patterns.text:
German will move almost anything to the front of a sentence, and the verb stays in second place regardless. Whatever got moved, the subject goes behind the verb to make room.

• Ich **gehe** heute in die Stadt.
• Heute **gehe** ich in die Stadt.
• In die Stadt **gehe** ich heute.

All three are correct and they emphasise different things. What is never correct is *Heute ich gehe*, which is the one an English speaker reaches for first.

Second **position**, not second word. "Der alte Mann" is one position.

patterns.title: Verbs that come apart
patterns.text:
Some verbs have a front half that detaches and goes to the end of the sentence. You have been reading it happen for sixteen stories.

• ankommen → Der Zug **kommt** in Luzern **an**.
• aussteigen → Ich **steige** langsam **aus**.
• mitkommen → **Kommen** Sie **mit**.

The longer the sentence, the further apart they get, and the meaning is not finished until that last word lands. This is why Germans seem to be waiting for the end of your sentence. They are.

You do not have to learn a list. You have to notice the stray little word at the end and put it back on the front.

patterns.title: kein or nicht
patterns.text:
Two ways to say no, and they are not interchangeable.

**kein** cancels a noun. It replaces ein.
• Ich habe **keinen** Schirm.
• Es gibt **kein** Brot mehr.

**nicht** cancels everything else — a verb, an adjective, a whole sentence.
• Ich verstehe **nicht**.
• Der Laden ist **nicht** offen.

The test: if the thing you are cancelling could have had *ein* in front of it, use kein.

patterns.title: Sie and du
patterns.text:
Two ways of saying "you", and picking wrong is louder than a grammar mistake.

**Sie** — a stranger, anybody older, a shopkeeper, an official. Capital S, always. *Kommen Sie mit. Wo wohnen Sie?*

**du** — friends, people your own age once you know them, children, family. *Kommst du mit? Wo wohnst du?*

You start with Sie and you wait. The other person offers du when they are ready, and in Switzerland that can take a while — being offered it is a small event, not a formality.

Being too formal costs nothing. Being too familiar with somebody who is seventy costs a surprising amount.

patterns.title: Franken, Rappen and the .95
patterns.text:
One franc is a hundred Rappen, and nothing smaller than five Rappen exists any more.

• **4.50** is said *vier Franken fünfzig*, or just *vier fünfzig*
• **3.95** is *drei Franken fünfundneunzig*

Prices ending .95 are everywhere and they are doing the same job as .99 anywhere else.

Cash still works everywhere and nobody thinks twice about it. What does get noticed is handing over a fifty for a four-franc coffee. Break your notes when you get the chance.

patterns.title: halb acht is half past SEVEN
patterns.text:
The one that catches every English speaker, and it catches them at a station.

German counts **towards** the coming hour, not away from the one just gone.

• **halb acht** = 7:30, half way to eight
• **Viertel vor acht** = 7:45
• **Viertel nach acht** = 8:15

A timetable will say *acht Uhr dreissig* and be perfectly clear. A person will say *halb acht* and mean the same moment.

**Punkt acht** means eight exactly, and here that is not a figure of speech.

patterns.title: The Swiss word, not the German one
patterns.text:
Some everyday things simply have a different name here, and using the German German one marks you out faster than an accent does.

• **Billett**, not Fahrkarte
• **Perron**, not Bahnsteig
• **Gipfeli**, not Hörnchen
• **Weggli**, not Brötchen
• **Sack**, not Tüte
• **Spital**, not Krankenhaus
• **Velo**, not Fahrrad

A lot of them came in through French, which is why so many look like it. They are not slang and they are not dialect. They are what the newspaper prints.

And there is no **ß** in Switzerland at all. Strasse, gross, heisst. Ever.

patterns.title: Long words are short words stuck together
patterns.text:
German glues nouns end to end and calls the result one word. This looks like the hardest thing about the language and it is one of the easiest.

• Bahn + Hof = **Bahnhof**, the train yard
• Flug + Hafen = **Flughafen**, the flight harbour
• Fahr + Plan = **Fahrplan**, the going plan
• Trink + Wasser = **Trinkwasser**

**The last piece is the word.** A Fahrplan is a plan. A Rolltreppe is a staircase. Everything in front of it is a description.

So you never have to be taught Vierwaldstättersee. Four, forest places, lake. It is a lake.

patterns.title: müssen, dürfen, können — and the verb that gets sent to the end
patterns.text:
Five little verbs, and the whole Hausordnung is written out of three of them.

• **müssen** — you have to. *Ich muss die Miete bezahlen.*
• **dürfen** — you are allowed to. *Man darf nach zehn nicht duschen.*
• **können** — you are able to. *Ich kann selber putzen.*
• **wollen** — you want to. *Ich will keine Probleme.*
• **sollen** — you are supposed to. *Man soll die Treppe putzen.*

**The real verb goes to the END of the clause, and it goes there as an infinitive.** *Ich muss die Wohnung sehr gut **putzen**.* Everything else piles up in the middle and the meaning does not finish until that last word lands.

You have seen this bracket before: it is the same one a separable verb makes. German opens something at position two and closes it at the end, and once you hear the opening you are waiting for the close.

**darf nicht is a prohibition, muss nicht is not.** *Du darfst nicht* means you may not. *Du musst nicht* means you do not have to.

patterns.title: der becomes den, and nothing else moves
patterns.text:
A German noun changes with its job in the sentence. The first change worth learning is the accusative — the thing the verb is done TO.

**And it is smaller than it looks. Only the masculine moves.**

• der Tisch → Ich nehme **den** Tisch.
• ein Stuhl → Ich kaufe **einen** Stuhl.
• kein Velo → Ich habe **kein** Velo. *(neuter, unchanged)*
• die Wohnung → Ich putze **die** Wohnung. *(feminine, unchanged)*
• das Bad → Ich sehe **das** Bad. *(neuter, unchanged)*

Three of the four do nothing at all. Learn **der → den** and **ein → einen** and you have most of it.

This is why the article has to be learned welded to the noun. If you do not know a Tisch is *der*, you cannot know it becomes *den* — and that is the mistake that never goes away on its own.

patterns.title: man — the word every rule is written in
patterns.text:
**man** is not *ein Mann*. It means people-in-general, the way English says "you" without meaning you personally.

• *Man darf hier nicht rauchen.* — no smoking here.
• *Man muss sich eintragen.* — you have to sign up.
• *Das macht man so.* — that is how it is done.

It takes the same verb form as *er*: man **darf**, man **muss**, man **macht**.

**Every rule in this country is written with it.** The Hausordnung, the signs at the Sammelstelle, the notice in the Waschküche. Nobody is being told off and nobody is named — the rule simply exists and applies to everybody. That is very Swiss, and once you hear it you hear it everywhere.

patterns.title: seit — where German uses the present and English does not
patterns.text:
Something that started in the past and is STILL GOING takes the **present tense** in German. English insists on a past form here, and that mismatch is one of the commonest mistakes learners make in both directions.

• *Ich wohne seit einem Monat hier.* — I **have been** living here a month.
• *Er arbeitet seit elf Jahren dort.* — he **has** worked there eleven years.
• *Sie wohnt seit vierzig Jahren im gleichen Haus.*

Say *ich habe gewohnt* and a German speaker understands that you have stopped.

**seit takes the dative**, which is why it is *seit einem Monat* and not *seit ein Monat*. That is worth noticing now and not worrying about yet.

patterns.title: The shoes come off. Nobody will ask you.
patterns.text:
You take your shoes off at the door. Your own flat, somebody else’s flat, it makes no difference.

**Nobody asks and nobody offers.** The caretaker does it. The men delivering your furniture do it. The neighbour coming up to complain about the noise does it — he climbs two floors in his socks to knock on your door.

There is no sentence for this. There is a small pile of shoes by every front door and you add yours to it.

Keeping them on is not rude in a loud way. It is the sort of thing nobody mentions and everybody notices, which is the most Swiss category of mistake there is.

patterns.title: Four bins, and one of them costs money
patterns.text:
Everything gets separated, and it is not only about the environment.

• **Glas** → the Sammelstelle, sorted by colour: white, brown, green
• **PET** and **Alu** → back to the shop
• **Papier** and **Karton** → out on the street, flat and tied with string, on their own day
• **Kehricht** → the Gebührensack, and only that bag

**Here is the part that explains the rest.** Glass, paper and PET cost nothing. The Kehricht costs, because you pay for its collection in the price of the bag — over two francs a bag. Anybody with a lot of rubbish pays a lot.

So separating carefully is not virtue, it is arithmetic. That is why everybody does it, and why the wrong bag gets opened, looked into, and left on the pavement with a sticker on it.

patterns.title: Everything is an Abo, and every Abo has a Frist
patterns.text:
The phone, the train, the gym, the newspaper, the insurance. All of it is an **Abo** and all of it renews itself.

Two words decide everything, and they are the two to find before you sign:

• **die Dauer** — how long it runs. Twenty-four months is normal.
• **die Frist** — how long before the end you have to give notice. Three months is normal.

**kündigen** is the verb. Not cancelling — giving notice, in writing, in time. Miss the Frist by a day and it runs another year.

A phone for one franc is not a phone for one franc. It is a phone paid for in twenty-four small pieces, and that is in the contract, which is why reading it matters more here than the price does.

patterns.title: Bills come on paper, and they have a deadline
patterns.text:
Not by email. On paper, into the letterbox, with a QR code in the bottom right corner.

Everything is in that code — the account, the amount, your name. Hold your phone over it, or put the bill into the machine at the post office, or queue at the counter and pay in cash. All three are normal.

**Three words to read first:**
• **der Betrag** — the amount
• **das Datum** — the deadline, usually thirty days
• **die Mahnung** — what arrives if you miss it, and it costs twenty francs

The habit everybody here has: the bill comes, you pay it the same day, it goes in the folder. Not because anybody is virtuous, but because a Mahnung is expensive and a second one is worse.

I see another meadow.
I see a lot of meadows.
There are trees between the meadows.
Then there is water.
I see a lake.

sn.s: Der See ist lang und schmal.
sn.e: The lake is long and narrow.

sn.s: Auf dem See ist ein Boot.
sn.e: There is a boat on the lake.
The boat is moving slowly.
The train is moving fast.
The train stops in Zug.
The town is called Zug.

sn.s: Zug ist auch das Wort für den Zug.
sn.e: Zug is also the word for a train.
A train stops in Zug.
I like that.

sn.s: Der Mann neben mir steht auf.
sn.e: The man next to me stands up.
He says Ade and leaves.
Now I am sitting on my own.
I sit and look.
The journey is calm.

sn.s: Eine Fahrt am Morgen ist immer ruhig.
sn.e: A morning journey is always calm.
Suddenly it is dark.

sn.s: Der Zug fährt durch einen Tunnel.
sn.e: The train goes through a tunnel.
In the tunnel I see nothing.

sn.s: Im Fenster sehe ich nur mich.
sn.e: In the window I only see myself.
The tunnel goes on for a long time.

sn.s: Dann ist der Tunnel zu Ende.
sn.e: Then the tunnel ends.

sn.s: Nach dem Tunnel ist alles hell.
sn.e: After the tunnel everything is bright.
I see meadows again.

sn.s: Und dann sehe ich wieder Wasser.
sn.e: And then I see water again.
It is a different lake.
This lake is wide.
There are mountains behind the lake.
The mountains are high.

sn.s: Oben auf den Bergen liegt Schnee.
sn.e: There is snow on top of the mountains.

sn.s: Es ist September und da liegt Schnee.
sn.e: It is September and there is snow up there.

sn.s: Ich schaue aus dem Fenster und sage nichts.
sn.e: I look out of the window and say nothing.

sn.s: Ich bin still wie alle anderen.
sn.e: I am as quiet as everyone else.
An hour goes quickly.
The hour is almost over.
A voice says something.
Next stop Luzern.
I understand those two words.
The people stand up.
They take their bags.
I take my suitcase.
The train slows down.

sn.s: Vor dem Fenster kommt der See wieder.
sn.e: The lake comes back in front of the window.

sn.s: Der Zug fährt fast im Wasser.
sn.e: The train runs almost in the water.
Then I see houses.
Then I see a roof.
Then the train stops.
The journey is over.
One hour and five minutes.

sn.s: Genau eine Stunde und fünf Minuten.
sn.e: Exactly one hour and five minutes.
I sit for another moment.
Then I stand up.
I go to the door.
Nobody talks.
It is still quiet.

sn.s: Ich schaue ein letztes Mal aus dem Fenster.
sn.e: I look out of the window one last time.
Meadows, a tunnel, two lakes.
An hour of Switzerland.

lessons.title: Angekommen
lessons.desc: A station with an old gate standing in front of it

sn.s: Der Zug kommt in Luzern an.
sn.e: The train arrives in Luzern.
I arrive in Luzern.

sn.s: Ich komme mit einem Koffer an.
sn.e: I arrive with one suitcase.
The people get off.
I get off too.
I get off slowly.
The suitcase is heavy.

sn.s: Ich stelle ihn auf den Boden.
sn.e: I put it down on the ground.
The ground is wet.
It is raining a little.
I stand on the platform.
So here I am.
This is where I stay now.
The people walk fast.
I wait for a moment.
I wait and look.
The station is big.
The roof is made of glass.
The station is new.
I pick the suitcase up again.
I walk to the hall.

sn.s: In der Halle sind viele Leute.
sn.e: There are a lot of people in the hall.
Some are waiting.
Some are running.
A woman waits holding flowers.
She is waiting for somebody.
Nobody is waiting for me.
That is all right too.
I go outside.
It is cool outside.
Outside it is raining lightly.

sn.s: Vor dem Bahnhof ist ein Platz.
sn.e: There is a square in front of the station.

sn.s: Auf dem Platz steht ein Tor.
sn.e: There is a gate standing on the square.
The gate is big.
The gate is made of stone.
The stone is grey.
The stone is old.
The gate stands there on its own.
There is nothing behind the gate.

sn.s: Es ist ein Tor ohne Haus.
sn.e: It is a gate with no building.
I do not understand it.
I walk through the gate.

sn.s: Auf der anderen Seite ist der Platz.
sn.e: On the other side is the square.
The gate leads nowhere.
A man sees me.
He says Grüezi.
I say Grüezi.
He points at the gate.

sn.s: Hier steht der alte Bahnhof nicht mehr, sagt er.
sn.e: The old station does not stand here any more, he says.
In nineteen seventy-one the station burns.

sn.s: Das Feuer nimmt den ganzen Bahnhof.
sn.e: The fire takes the whole station.

sn.s: Nach dem Feuer bleibt nur das Tor.
sn.e: After the fire only the gate is left.

sn.s: Das Feuer nimmt alles ausser dem Stein.
sn.e: The fire takes everything except the stone.

sn.s: Ein Feuer nimmt kein Tor aus Stein.
sn.e: A fire does not take a gate made of stone.

sn.s: Vom Feuer sieht man heute nichts mehr.
sn.e: Today you can see nothing of the fire.
Merci, I say.
The man goes.

sn.s: Ich schaue das Tor noch einmal an.
sn.e: I look at the gate again.

sn.s: Jetzt ist es kein leeres Tor mehr.
sn.e: Now it is not an empty gate any more.

sn.s: Der Stein ist der Rest von einem Haus.
sn.e: The stone is what is left of a building.
I picture it.
There stands the old station.

sn.s: Dort warten Leute und dort kommen Züge an.
sn.e: There people wait and there trains arrive.

sn.s: Hier ist jetzt nur der Platz.
sn.e: Now there is only the square here.

sn.s: Ich stelle den Koffer auf den Boden.
sn.e: I put the suitcase down on the ground.
The ground is made of stone.

sn.s: Ich setze mich auf den Koffer.
sn.e: I sit down on the suitcase.
I wait.
I am waiting for nothing.
Outside buses are driving past.

sn.s: Die Busse sind gelb und blau.
sn.e: The buses are yellow and blue.
The lake is over there.
I can see water over there.
Here it smells of rain.

sn.s: Hier ist es laut und ruhig zugleich.
sn.e: Here it is loud and calm at the same time.

sn.s: Eine Frau steigt aus einem Bus aus.
sn.e: A woman gets off a bus.
A child gets off too.

sn.s: Sie steigen aus und gehen weiter.
sn.e: They get off and walk on.

sn.s: Niemand bleibt lang auf dem Platz.
sn.e: Nobody stays long on the square.
Only I stay.
I wait another five minutes.
Then I wait another five.
The rain stops.
Outside it gets bright.
I stand up.

sn.s: Ich nehme den Koffer vom Boden.
sn.e: I pick the suitcase up off the ground.

sn.s: Ich gehe durch das Tor zurück.
sn.e: I walk back through the gate.
Then I head over to the lake.
A train arrives.
People get off.

sn.s: Das geht den ganzen Tag so.
sn.e: That goes on all day.
I arrive today.
Tomorrow somebody else arrives.

sn.s: Das Tor steht und schaut zu.
sn.e: The gate stands there and watches.
The stone says nothing.

lessons.title: Ein Kaffee, bitte
lessons.desc: The first thing you order on purpose

sn.e: There is a café on the square.
I go in.
The café is small.
It is small and warm.
Four people are sitting inside.
They are all sitting.
Nobody is standing and drinking.

sn.s: Hier trinkt man den Kaffee im Sitzen.
sn.e: Here you drink your coffee sitting down.

sn.s: Ich stelle den Koffer neben einen Tisch.
sn.e: I put the suitcase down next to a table.
I sit down.
A woman comes over.
She is young.
She says Grüezi.
I say Grüezi.
Her name is Lea.

sn.s: Ihr Name steht auf ihrer Schürze.
sn.e: Her name is on her apron.
Lea asks something.

sn.s: Ich verstehe die Frage nicht ganz.
sn.e: I do not quite understand the question.
I would like a coffee.
I say: a coffee, please.
Bitte is a good word.
Lea asks: a crème?
I do not know the word.
She asks again, slowly.
A Kaffee crème?
I say yes.
She says gladly.

sn.s: Gern heisst: das mache ich gern.
sn.e: Gern means: I am happy to.
Lea goes to the machine.
I hear the machine.
It smells good.
She comes back with a cup.
The cup is small.
The cup is very small.

sn.s: Zu Hause ist eine Tasse gross.
sn.e: At home a cup is big.
Here the cup is small.

sn.s: Auf der Tasse liegt ein Löffel.
sn.e: There is a spoon on the cup.
Next to it lies a piece of chocolate.
The coffee is hot.
It is very hot.
I wait a moment.
The coffee stays hot for a long time.

sn.s: Lea bringt auch ein Glas Wasser.
sn.e: Lea also brings a glass of water.
You do not order the water.
It simply comes with it.
Merci, I say.
Lea says bitte.
Here bitte means: you are welcome.
Bitte has two meanings.

sn.s: Man sagt bitte und man bekommt bitte.
sn.e: You say bitte and you get bitte back.
There is sugar on the table.

sn.s: Der Zucker ist in kleinen Päckchen.
sn.e: The sugar is in little packets.
I take one packet of sugar.
I do not want much sugar.
A little sugar is enough.

sn.s: Ich rühre den Zucker in den Kaffee.
sn.e: I stir the sugar into the coffee.
The coffee is good.
The coffee is really good.

sn.s: Er ist stark und nicht bitter.
sn.e: It is strong and not bitter.
I drink slowly.
Nobody is in a hurry.

sn.s: Am Tisch daneben sitzt ein alter Mann.
sn.e: An old man is sitting at the next table.
He is reading the newspaper.

sn.s: Vor ihm steht eine kleine Tasse.
sn.e: There is a small cup in front of him.
The cup is already empty.
He is still sitting there anyway.
Lea comes back.
She asks: anything else?

sn.s: Ich möchte gern noch einen Kaffee.
sn.e: I would like another coffee.
But I say nothing.
Then I order one after all.
Another coffee, please.
Lea laughs a little.
Another crème, she says.
She says it kindly.

sn.s: Sie sagt nicht: das heisst Crème.
sn.e: She does not say: it is called crème.
She just says the word.

sn.s: Ich höre es und ich behalte es.
sn.e: I hear it and I keep it.

sn.s: Beim zweiten Mal bestelle ich richtig.
sn.e: The second time I order it right.
I order a crème.
That is how you order it here.

sn.s: Die zweite Tasse ist auch klein.
sn.e: The second cup is small too.
It is hot too.

sn.s: So heiss trinke ich ihn gern.
sn.e: That is how hot I like to drink it.
I do not take any more sugar.

sn.s: Ohne Zucker ist er auch gut.
sn.e: It is good without sugar too.

sn.s: Ich sitze und trinke und schaue.
sn.e: I sit and drink and look.
Outside people walk past.
Inside it is warm.
I would like to stay here a bit longer.
I do not want to move on yet.
Lea asks: where are you from?
I tell her.
She does not ask anything else.
I like that.
I say: merci vielmal.
Lea says: gladly, Ade.
Ade, I say.

sn.s: Ein Kaffee, eine Tasse, ein Wort.
sn.e: A coffee, a cup, one word.
Crème.
I am keeping that one.

lessons.title: Gipfeli
lessons.desc: Bread has different names here

sn.e: In the morning I am hungry.
I look for a bakery.

sn.s: Die Bäckerei ist gleich um die Ecke.
sn.e: The bakery is just around the corner.
The bakery is open already.
It is only half past six.

sn.s: Eine Bäckerei macht hier früh auf.
sn.e: A bakery opens early here.
I go in.
It smells of bread.
The bread lies on the shelf.
There is a lot of bread.
Big bread and small bread.
The bread is fresh.
Everything is fresh.
Fresh means: from this morning.

sn.s: Hinter dem Glas liegen kleine Sachen.
sn.e: Behind the glass lie small things.
I do not know the names.

sn.s: Eine Frau fragt: was möchten Sie?
sn.e: A woman asks: what would you like?
I point at something round.

sn.s: Ich zeige, denn ich habe das Wort nicht.
sn.e: I point, because I do not have the word.
Pointing always works.
The woman says: a Weggli?
A Weggli, I say.

sn.s: Ein Weggli ist ein kleines weiches Brot.
sn.e: A Weggli is a small soft roll.
It is white and round.
In Germany it is called something else.
Here it is called a Weggli.

sn.s: Ich sage das Wort noch einmal.
sn.e: I say the word again.
Weggli.

sn.s: Dann zeige ich auf etwas anderes.
sn.e: Then I point at something else.
It is brown and curved.
The woman says: a Gipfeli.
A Gipfeli, I say.

sn.s: Das Gipfeli ist krumm wie ein Mond.
sn.e: The Gipfeli is curved like a moon.

sn.s: Es ist aussen hart und innen weich.
sn.e: It is hard outside and soft inside.

sn.s: Ein Gipfeli ist nicht sehr gross.
sn.e: A Gipfeli is not very big.
I take a Gipfeli.
I take a Weggli too.
And I take a loaf of bread.
The bread is for later.

sn.s: Die Frau fragt: sonst noch etwas?
sn.e: The woman asks: anything else?
No, merci, I say.
I buy three things.

sn.s: Ich kaufe hier jeden Morgen etwas.
sn.e: I buy something here every morning.
I do not buy much.
Buying goes quickly here.

sn.s: Sie legt alles in einen Sack.
sn.e: She puts everything in a bag.
The bag is made of paper.
I pay and say merci.
She says: merci vielmal, Ade.

sn.s: Draussen setze ich mich auf eine Bank.
sn.e: Outside I sit down on a bench.
I eat the Gipfeli first.
It is still warm.
I eat slowly.

sn.s: Das Gipfeli ist besser als das Weggli.
sn.e: The Gipfeli is better than the Weggli.

sn.s: Ich zeige auf etwas und bekomme etwas Besseres.
sn.e: I point at something and get something better.
Then I eat the Weggli.
The Weggli is soft.

sn.s: Ein Weggli isst man einfach so.
sn.e: You just eat a Weggli as it is.
You do not need anything with it.
I do not eat the bread.
The bread stays in the bag.

sn.s: Um acht gehe ich noch einmal vorbei.
sn.e: At eight I walk past again.
I look through the window.
The shelf is almost empty.
The Gipfeli are gone.
No more Gipfeli.
The Weggli are gone too.

sn.s: Nur ein Brot liegt noch da.
sn.e: Only one loaf is still lying there.
In the afternoon everything is gone.
A bakery bakes in the morning.
Gone is gone.

sn.s: Man geht früh oder man geht umsonst.
sn.e: You go early or you go for nothing.

sn.s: Das lerne ich am ersten Tag.
sn.e: I learn that on the first day.

sn.s: Am zweiten Morgen bin ich um sieben da.
sn.e: On the second morning I am there at seven.
I do not have to point any more.

sn.s: Ich sage: ein Gipfeli und zwei Weggli, bitte.
sn.e: I say: one Gipfeli and two Weggli, please.
The woman nods.
She does not ask anything.

sn.s: Sie nimmt ein Gipfeli und zwei Weggli.
sn.e: She takes one Gipfeli and two Weggli.
Everything is fresh.

sn.s: Ich kaufe wieder ein Brot dazu.
sn.e: I buy a loaf again as well.

sn.s: Das Brot ist gross und dunkel.
sn.e: The bread is big and dark.
It does not cost much.

sn.s: Ich esse ein Weggli auf dem Weg.
sn.e: I eat one Weggli on the way.

sn.s: Das zweite Weggli esse ich später.
sn.e: The second Weggli I eat later.

sn.s: Am dritten Morgen sagt die Frau Grüezi zu mir.
sn.e: On the third morning the woman says Grüezi to me.

sn.s: Sie sagt es anders als am ersten Tag.
sn.e: She says it differently from the first day.

sn.s: Sie kennt mich jetzt ein bisschen.
sn.e: She knows me a little now.

sn.s: Das Gipfeli, sagt sie, und lacht.
sn.e: The Gipfeli, she says, and laughs.
Yes, I say. The Gipfeli.

sn.s: Ich nehme es und ich bezahle.
sn.e: I take it and I pay.
I eat it outside.

sn.s: Es ist frisch und es ist warm.
sn.e: It is fresh and it is warm.
Three mornings, three Gipfeli.

sn.s: Ein Wort mehr an jedem Tag.
sn.e: One more word every day.

lessons.title: Franken und Rappen
lessons.desc: Money that is not yours yet

sn.e: I have money.

sn.s: Aber das Geld ist mir fremd.
sn.e: But the money is strange to me.
Here the money is called francs.
One franc has a hundred Rappen.

sn.s: Der Rappen ist der kleine Teil.
sn.e: The Rappen is the small part.
A hundred Rappen make one franc.

sn.s: Ich habe eine Note in der Hand.
sn.e: I have a note in my hand.
The note is yellow.
The note says fifty.
Fifty francs.
The note is beautiful.

sn.s: Sie ist kleiner als eine Note von zu Hause.
sn.e: It is smaller than a note from home.
I also have coins.
The coins are heavy.

sn.s: Eine Münze ist gross und silbern.
sn.e: One coin is big and silver.
The coin says five.
That is five francs.

sn.s: Eine kleine Münze ist zwanzig Rappen.
sn.e: A small coin is twenty Rappen.

sn.s: Die kleinste Münze ist fünf Rappen.
sn.e: The smallest coin is five Rappen.

sn.s: Weniger als fünf Rappen gibt es nicht.
sn.e: There is nothing smaller than five Rappen.
I go into the café.
Lea says Grüezi.
I order a crème.
I want to know the price.
I ask: what does that cost?
Lea points at the menu.

sn.s: Auf der Karte steht der Preis.
sn.e: The price is on the menu.

sn.s: Der Preis ist vier Franken fünfzig.
sn.e: The price is four francs fifty.
That is a normal price.

sn.s: Ein Kaffee kostet hier vier oder fünf Franken.
sn.e: A coffee here costs four or five francs.
At home it costs less.
Here everything is expensive.
Really everything is expensive.

sn.s: Aber die Leute sagen nichts dazu.
sn.e: But people do not say anything about it.

sn.s: Für sie ist es kein teurer Preis.
sn.e: For them it is not an expensive price.
I look at other prices.

sn.s: Ein Preis endet oft auf fünfundneunzig.
sn.e: A price often ends in ninety-five.
Three francs ninety-five.
Nine francs ninety-five.

sn.s: Fünfundneunzig Rappen sind fast ein Franken.
sn.e: Ninety-five Rappen is almost a franc.
But it looks smaller.
They do that everywhere.
I have to pay.
Paying goes quickly here.
I give Lea the note.
Fifty francs for one coffee.
Lea takes the note.
She looks at me.
She does not say anything.
But she looks for a moment.
I notice it.

sn.s: Fünfzig Franken sind zu viel für vier Franken fünfzig.
sn.e: Fifty francs is too much for four francs fifty.

sn.s: Sie gibt mir viel Geld zurück.
sn.e: She gives me a lot of money back.
She counts it out loud.
Five, ten, twenty, forty-five fifty.
I get two notes back.

sn.s: Und ich bekomme viele Münzen zurück.
sn.e: And I get a lot of coins back.

sn.s: Zurück heisst: der Rest vom Geld.
sn.e: Back means: the rest of the money.

sn.s: Ich stecke das Geld zurück in die Tasche.
sn.e: I put the money back in my pocket.
My pocket is heavy now.

sn.s: Beim nächsten Mal bezahle ich klein.
sn.e: Next time I will pay with something small.
I pay with coins.

sn.s: Ich lege vier Franken fünfzig hin.
sn.e: I put down four francs fifty.

sn.s: Zwei Münzen zu zwei Franken und eine halbe.
sn.e: Two two-franc coins and a half.
Lea says merci.
This time she does not look.
She does not have to give anything back.

sn.s: Ich bekomme nichts zurück und das ist gut so.
sn.e: I get nothing back and that is how it should be.
That is better.

sn.s: Ich zahle fast immer mit Geld in der Hand.
sn.e: I nearly always pay with cash in hand.

sn.s: Man kann hier überall so bezahlen.
sn.e: You can pay that way everywhere here.

sn.s: Auch im Laden und im Zug.
sn.e: In the shop and on the train too.
Nobody looks at you oddly.

sn.s: Am Abend zähle ich mein Geld.
sn.e: In the evening I count my money.

sn.s: Ich lege die Noten auf den Tisch.
sn.e: I put the notes on the table.
I put the coins next to them.

sn.s: Ich habe hundert Franken und ein bisschen.
sn.e: I have a hundred francs and a bit.
That is not much here.
A week costs more.
The room costs the most.
Food costs a lot too.

sn.s: Der Kaffee ist teuer, aber er ist gut.
sn.e: The coffee is expensive, but it is good.

sn.s: Das Billett ist teuer, aber der Zug ist pünktlich.
sn.e: The ticket is expensive, but the train is on time.
Maybe that is the deal.

sn.s: Ich nehme eine Münze in die Hand.
sn.e: I take a coin in my hand.
Twenty Rappen.
So small and so heavy.

sn.s: Ich lerne die Münzen mit den Augen.
sn.e: I learn the coins by sight.

sn.s: Gross und silbern ist fünf Franken.
sn.e: Big and silver is five francs.

sn.s: Klein und golden ist zehn Rappen.
sn.e: Small and golden is ten Rappen.

sn.s: Bald muss ich nicht mehr schauen.
sn.e: Soon I will not have to look any more.

sn.s: Bald fühle ich das Geld in der Hand.
sn.e: Soon I will feel the money in my hand.
Francs and Rappen.

sn.s: Das Geld gehört mir noch nicht.
sn.e: The money is not mine yet.
But it will be.

lessons.title: Migros oder Coop
lessons.desc: Two shops, and there are only two

sn.e: I need food.
I need a lot of things.
I go shopping.
On Saturday everybody does their shopping.
Shopping is expensive here.

sn.s: Ich kaufe einmal in der Woche ein.
sn.e: I do my shopping once a week.
I look for a shop.
I find two shops.
One shop is called Migros.
The other shop is called Coop.
Migros is orange.
Coop is orange and red.

sn.s: Es gibt fast nur diese zwei.
sn.e: There are almost only these two.

sn.s: In jedem Dorf ist ein Migros oder ein Coop.
sn.e: In every village there is a Migros or a Coop.
Sometimes both.
I go into the Migros.

sn.s: Der Laden ist gross und hell.
sn.e: The shop is big and bright.
Everything is on the shelf.
Every shelf has a sign.
I read the signs.
I understand half of them.
First I need bread.
Then I need cheese.

sn.s: Der Käse ist in einem grossen Regal.
sn.e: The cheese is on a big shelf.
There is a great deal of cheese.
Too much cheese.
I do not know the names.

sn.s: Ich nehme einen Käse ohne Namen.
sn.e: I take a cheese with no name.
It is hard and yellow.
The cheese is expensive.
But you need cheese.
On the next shelf there is chocolate.

sn.s: Es gibt auch sehr viel Schokolade.
sn.e: There is a great deal of chocolate too.
A whole shelf of chocolate.
Brown, white and dark chocolate.
The chocolate is not expensive.

sn.s: Sie kostet weniger als der Käse.
sn.e: It costs less than the cheese.
I do not need chocolate.
I take one anyway.
Then I look for wine.

sn.s: Ich gehe durch den ganzen Laden.
sn.e: I walk through the whole shop.
I do not find any wine.
No shelf has wine.
I look again.
Still no wine.

sn.s: Ich frage einen Mann vom Laden.
sn.e: I ask a man who works in the shop.
Grüezi, where is the wine?
The man laughs briefly.

sn.s: Er sagt: bei uns gibt es keinen Wein.
sn.e: He says: we do not have any wine.
Migros does not sell wine.
It does not sell any alcohol at all.
Never, he says. Not ever.

sn.s: Das ist von Anfang an so.
sn.e: It is that way from the start.

sn.s: Der Mann vom Migros will das so.
sn.e: The man who started Migros wants it that way.

sn.s: Für Wein muss ich in den Coop.
sn.e: For wine I have to go to the Coop.
Merci vielmal, I say.
I go to the till.

sn.s: An der Kasse steht schon jemand.
sn.e: Somebody is already at the till.

sn.s: An der Kasse steht eine Frau.
sn.e: There is a woman at the till.
She says Grüezi.

sn.s: Sie zieht alles über das Glas.
sn.e: She pulls everything over the glass.
It goes very fast.

sn.s: An der Kasse geht alles schnell.
sn.e: Everything is fast at the till.
I do not have a bag.
I ask for a bag.
The bag costs something too.
A bag is not free.

sn.s: Die Leute bringen ihren eigenen Sack mit.
sn.e: People bring their own bag.
I keep forgetting that.
Forgetting is expensive here.
I pay and pack up.

sn.s: Am Freitag kaufe ich wieder ein.
sn.e: On Friday I do the shopping again.
I pack it myself.

sn.s: Niemand hilft mir, und das ist normal.
sn.e: Nobody helps me, and that is normal.

sn.s: Draussen schaue ich in den Sack.
sn.e: Outside I look in the bag.
Bread, cheese, chocolate.
No wine.

sn.s: Ich gehe für Wein in den Laden und komme mit Schokolade heraus.
sn.e: I go to the shop for wine and come out with chocolate.
I forget the milk as well.

sn.s: Die Milch vergesse ich jedes Mal.
sn.e: I forget the milk every single time.

sn.s: Der Coop ist zwei Strassen weiter.
sn.e: The Coop is two streets further on.
I walk over.
In the Coop there is wine.
A whole shelf of wine.
A lot of wine from Switzerland.
I do not know any of it.

sn.s: Ich nehme eine Flasche und schaue den Preis an.
sn.e: I take a bottle and look at the price.
The wine is expensive too.
I put the bottle back.
I take a cheaper one.
I take milk too.

sn.s: Diesmal vergesse ich die Milch nicht.
sn.e: This time I do not forget the milk.

sn.s: An der Kasse bezahle ich mit Münzen.
sn.e: At the till I pay with coins.

sn.s: Ich habe meinen Sack schon dabei.
sn.e: I have my bag with me already.
Two shops for one lot of shopping.
Migros for everything.
Coop for the wine.
Now I know.

lessons.title: Das Wasser ist gratis
lessons.desc: You can drink from the fountains

sn.s: Es ist warm und ich habe Durst.
sn.e: It is warm and I am thirsty.
I am very thirsty.
I would like water.
I go into a shop.
I buy a bottle of water.
The bottle costs two francs.
Two francs for water.

sn.s: Ich trinke die halbe Flasche sofort.
sn.e: I drink half the bottle straight away.
Outside I sit down.

sn.s: Neben mir sitzt eine alte Frau.
sn.e: An old woman is sitting next to me.
She says Grüezi.
I say Grüezi.
She looks at my bottle.

sn.s: Sie fragt: kaufen Sie das Wasser?
sn.e: She asks: do you buy your water?
Yes, I say.
She points at the square.
There is a fountain over there.
The fountain is made of stone.
Water runs out of the fountain.
The water runs all the time.
It runs day and night.

sn.s: Das Wasser ist gratis, sagt sie.
sn.e: The water is free, she says.
Not much is free here.
Free means: it costs nothing.
She says it kindly.
She is not laughing at me.

sn.s: Sie sagt es, denn ich weiss es nicht.
sn.e: She says it, because I do not know.

sn.s: Kann man das trinken?, frage ich.
sn.e: Can you drink that?, I ask.
She says: yes, of course.
You can drink almost anywhere.
Almost every fountain is drinking water.

sn.s: Wenn nicht, dann steht es dran.
sn.e: If not, there is a sign on it.
Then it says: not drinking water.
Otherwise you can drink.

sn.s: Ich stehe auf und gehe zum Brunnen.
sn.e: I stand up and go to the fountain.
The fountain is old.
The water is cold.
It is very cold.
I hold my hand under it.

sn.s: Das Wasser läuft mir über die Hand.
sn.e: The water runs over my hand.
My hand goes cold at once.
I drink out of my hand.

sn.s: Aus der Hand schmeckt es am besten.
sn.e: Out of your hand it tastes best.
The water is clean.
It is very clean.
It tastes clean.
It tastes of nothing.
That is how water should taste.
I drink again.
I drink a lot.
My thirst is gone.
I fill my bottle up.
The bottle is full quickly.
Now it is completely full.
The bottle costs two francs.
The water in it is free.
I go back to the woman.
Merci vielmal, I say.

sn.s: Sie sagt: das macht jeder am Anfang.
sn.e: She says: everybody does that at the start.

sn.s: Dann sagt sie Ade und geht.
sn.e: Then she says Ade and leaves.

sn.s: In der Stadt sind viele Brunnen.
sn.e: There are a lot of fountains in the town.
Now I see them everywhere.

sn.s: Am ersten Tag sehe ich sie nicht.
sn.e: On the first day I do not see them.
A fountain on the corner.
A fountain in front of the church.

sn.s: Ein Brunnen mitten auf dem Platz.
sn.e: A fountain in the middle of the square.
Some fountains are very old.
Some have a figure standing on them.
Water runs out of all of them.
Children drink as they walk past.

sn.s: Ein Mann macht seine Flasche voll.
sn.e: A man fills his bottle up.

sn.s: Ein Hund trinkt unten aus dem Stein.
sn.e: A dog drinks from the stone at the bottom.
Nobody buys water.
Only new people buy water.
I am new here too.
Now I drink at the fountain.

sn.s: Ich trinke jeden Tag am Brunnen.
sn.e: I drink at the fountain every day.

sn.s: Ich habe die Flasche immer dabei.
sn.e: I always have the bottle with me.
It is always full.

sn.s: Ich mache sie voll und gehe weiter.
sn.e: I fill it up and walk on.
It costs nothing.
Everything here is expensive.
Only the water is free.

sn.s: Und es ist besser als das aus der Flasche.
sn.e: And it is better than the stuff from the bottle.

sn.s: Es ist kalt und sauber und es kostet nichts.
sn.e: It is cold and clean and it costs nothing.

sn.s: Es ist kälter und es ist sauberer.
sn.e: It is colder and it is cleaner.
I can drink anywhere.
I can always drink.

sn.s: Der Durst ist kein Problem mehr.
sn.e: Thirst is not a problem any more.

sn.s: Am Abend gehe ich am Brunnen vorbei.
sn.e: In the evening I walk past the fountain.
I am not thirsty.
I drink anyway.
The water keeps running.
It runs all night.
For nobody.
Or for everybody.

lessons.title: Wo ist die Post?
lessons.desc: Asking, and understanding half the answer

sn.e: I have to go to the post office.

sn.s: Ich weiss den Weg zur Post nicht.
sn.e: I do not know the way to the post office.
I walk through the town.
The streets are narrow.
Every street looks the same.
I walk up a street.

sn.s: Dann gehe ich die Strasse wieder hinunter.
sn.e: Then I walk back down the street.
I do not find the post office.
There are people standing on a square.
The square is small.

sn.s: Auf dem Platz ist ein Brunnen.
sn.e: There is a fountain on the square.
I ask a woman.
Grüezi, where is the post office?
The woman thinks for a moment.
Then she talks.
She talks fast.
She says: up ahead on the left.
Left I understand.

sn.s: Dann sagt sie etwas mit rechts.
sn.e: Then she says something with right in it.
Right I understand too.
Then she says straight on.
Straight on I understand too.

sn.s: Aber alles zusammen verstehe ich nicht.
sn.e: But all of it together I do not understand.

sn.s: Links, rechts, geradeaus, und dann noch etwas.
sn.e: Left, right, straight on, and then something else.
I understand half of it.
I say merci.
I set off.
I go straight on.
Then I go left.

sn.s: Dann stehe ich wieder auf einem Platz.
sn.e: Then I am standing on a square again.
It is a different square.
Or is it the same one?
I do not know.
I ask a man.
He is maybe sixty.

sn.s: Grüezi, wo ist die Post, bitte?
sn.e: Grüezi, where is the post office, please?

sn.s: Der Mann fängt an zu erklären.
sn.e: The man starts explaining.
He points right.
Then he points left.
Then he stops.
He looks at me.

sn.s: Ich verstehe nichts, und er sieht das.
sn.e: I do not understand, and he sees it.
He says: come with me.
I come along.

sn.s: Wir gehen zusammen und er kommt einfach mit.
sn.e: We walk together and he simply comes along.
I come along.
We walk together.
He does not walk fast.
The way is not far.
We walk down a street.
Then we go right.
Then right again.
Then straight on across a square.

sn.s: So finde ich den Weg nie allein.
sn.e: I would never find the way on my own like that.
He asks: where are you from?
I tell him.

sn.s: Er nickt und sagt nichts weiter.
sn.e: He nods and says nothing more.
We walk on.
Then he stops.
He points at a building.
The building is yellow.
It is completely yellow.
The post office is yellow.

sn.s: Das Zeichen ist gelb und schwarz.
sn.e: The sign is yellow and black.

sn.s: Die Post ist immer gelb, sagt er.
sn.e: The post office is always yellow, he says.

sn.s: Die Autos von der Post sind auch gelb.
sn.e: The post office vans are yellow too.

sn.s: Der Bus von der Post ist auch gelb.
sn.e: The post bus is yellow as well.
Look for yellow, he says.
I say merci vielmal.
He says: no trouble at all.

sn.s: Dann sagt er Ade und geht zurück.
sn.e: Then he says Ade and walks back.

sn.s: Er geht den ganzen Weg zurück.
sn.e: He walks the whole way back.
He does not need to come this way at all.

sn.s: Ich frage, und er kommt einfach mit.
sn.e: I ask, and he just comes along.

sn.s: Das machen die Leute hier so.
sn.e: That is what people do here.
They do not like explaining at length.
They would rather come with you.

sn.s: Kommen Sie mit ist hier eine ganze Erklärung.
sn.e: Come with me is a whole explanation here.

sn.s: In der Post ist es ruhig.
sn.e: Inside the post office it is quiet.
I take a number.
I wait for my number.
At the counter I say Grüezi.

sn.s: Ich verstehe die Frau am Schalter gut.
sn.e: I understand the woman at the counter well.
She talks slowly to me.

sn.s: Draussen schaue ich noch einmal auf die Strasse.
sn.e: Outside I look at the street once more.
I make a note of the way.

sn.s: Rechts, rechts, geradeaus, dann das gelbe Haus.
sn.e: Right, right, straight on, then the yellow building.

sn.s: Beim nächsten Mal finde ich den Weg.
sn.e: Next time I will find the way.

sn.s: Beim nächsten Mal frage ich niemanden.
sn.e: Next time I will not ask anybody.
Maybe that is a shame.

lessons.title: Der See
lessons.desc: Water with mountains standing behind it

sn.e: I walk down a street.

sn.s: Am Ende der Strasse ist Licht.
sn.e: At the end of the street there is light.
Then the lake comes.
The lake is suddenly there.
I stop walking.
I just stand there.
The lake is big.
It is very big.

sn.s: Ich sehe das andere Ufer kaum.
sn.e: I can hardly see the other shore.

sn.s: Das Wasser ist grün und blau.
sn.e: The water is green and blue.
It is completely calm.
There are mountains behind the lake.
The mountains are big.
One mountain is very close.
The mountain is called Pilatus.
It is grey and steep.

sn.s: Ein anderer Berg ist weiter weg.
sn.e: Another mountain is further away.

sn.s: Er ist weit weg und trotzdem gross.
sn.e: It is far away and big all the same.

sn.s: Weit weg sieht alles klein aus, nur die Berge nicht.
sn.e: Far away everything looks small, except the mountains.

sn.s: Oben auf dem Berg liegt Schnee.
sn.e: There is snow on top of the mountain.

sn.s: Über den Bergen hängt eine Wolke.
sn.e: There is a cloud hanging over the mountains.
The cloud hardly moves.
The cloud is white.
It hangs halfway up.

sn.s: Der Berg geht durch die Wolke.
sn.e: The mountain goes through the cloud.

sn.s: Oben ist der Berg wieder da.
sn.e: Above it the mountain is there again.
That is beautiful.
It really is beautiful.

sn.s: Schön ist ein kleines Wort dafür.
sn.e: Beautiful is a small word for it.
I go to the shore.
The shore is made of stone.
There are benches along the shore.
People are sitting on the benches.
They sit and look.

sn.s: Sie schauen alle auf den See.
sn.e: They are all looking at the lake.
I sit down too.

sn.s: Ich halte die Hand ins Wasser.
sn.e: I put my hand in the water.
The water is cold.
It is very cold.

sn.s: Der See ist im September noch kalt.
sn.e: The lake is still cold in September.

sn.s: Das Wasser kommt von den Bergen.
sn.e: The water comes from the mountains.
That is why it is cold.
People swim anyway.
A man is swimming far out.
He swims very far out.

sn.s: So weit möchte ich nicht schwimmen.
sn.e: I would not want to swim that far.
Birds are sitting on the water.

sn.s: Ein Vogel ist weiss und gross.
sn.e: One bird is white and big.

sn.s: Ein anderer Vogel ist schwarz und klein.
sn.e: Another bird is black and small.

sn.s: Der Vogel taucht und kommt wieder hoch.
sn.e: The bird dives and comes back up.
A bird comes over to me.
It wants bread.
I do not have any bread.
The bird goes away again.
Then a boat comes.
The boat is white.
It is big and old.
The boat goes slowly.
It comes to the shore.
People get off the boat.
Other people get on.

sn.s: Dann fährt das Schiff wieder weg.
sn.e: Then the boat leaves again.

sn.s: Ein Schiff fährt hier wie ein Bus.
sn.e: A boat here runs like a bus.

sn.s: Es hält in jedem Dorf am See.
sn.e: It stops in every village on the lake.

sn.s: Man kann mit dem Schiff zur Arbeit fahren.
sn.e: You can go to work by boat.
I like that a lot.

sn.s: Neben mir sitzt ein alter Mann.
sn.e: An old man is sitting next to me.
He says Grüezi.

sn.s: Ich frage: wie heisst der See?
sn.e: I ask: what is the lake called?
He says: Vierwaldstättersee.
That is a long word.
I say it back slowly.
Four forest places, he says.
Vier means four.
The lake belongs to four cantons.
Four cantons lie on the water.
Luzern is one of them.
That is why the lake is called that.

sn.s: Ein See und vier Namen daneben.
sn.e: One lake with four names beside it.
Merci, I say.

sn.s: Er schaut wieder auf das Wasser.
sn.e: He looks back at the water.

sn.s: Wir sitzen und sagen nichts mehr.
sn.e: We sit and say nothing more.
That is nice too.

sn.s: Am Abend ist es noch schöner.
sn.e: In the evening it is more beautiful still.
The sun goes down.
The mountain turns red.
The lake goes dark.
The cloud turns red too.
Then everything goes grey.
It gets cold.
The people go home.
I stay a little longer.

sn.s: Der See ist gross und ich bin klein.
sn.e: The lake is big and I am small.

sn.s: Das ist heute kein schlechtes Gefühl.
sn.e: Today that is not a bad feeling.

lessons.title: Die Kapellbrücke
lessons.desc: A wooden bridge with paintings in the roof

sn.e: There is a bridge on the lake.
The bridge is made of wood.
It goes over the water.
It does not go straight.
The bridge makes a bend.
It is called the Kapellbrücke.
The bridge has a roof.

sn.s: Das Dach ist auch aus Holz.
sn.e: The roof is made of wood too.

sn.s: Man geht im Trockenen über das Wasser.
sn.e: You cross the water in the dry.
Even when it is raining.
I walk onto the bridge.
The wood makes noises.
It is dark wood.
It smells of old wood.
I walk slowly.
There are pictures up in the roof.
The pictures are triangular.
They fit exactly into the roof.
I look up.
I look up for a long time.

sn.s: Ein Bild zeigt einen Mann mit einem Schwert.
sn.e: One picture shows a man with a sword.
One picture shows a boat.
One picture shows the town.
The pictures are old.
They are very old.
Some of the pictures are dark.
You can hardly see anything on them.

sn.s: An manchen Stellen hängt kein Bild.
sn.e: In some places there is no picture.
There is only wood there.
The empty wood is new.

sn.s: Es ist heller als das andere.
sn.e: It is lighter than the rest.
At first I do not understand why.
A woman is standing next to me.
She is looking up too.

sn.s: Sie sagt: neunzehnhundertdreiundneunzig brennt die Brücke.
sn.e: She says: in nineteen ninety-three the bridge burns.
A fire in the night.
Almost the whole bridge burns.
Many of the pictures are gone.

sn.s: Die Brücke ist heute zum Teil neu.
sn.e: Today the bridge is partly new.

sn.s: Das helle Holz ist das neue Holz.
sn.e: The light wood is the new wood.
The dark wood is old.
Looking up you can see it clearly.
Old and new side by side.
Merci, I say.

sn.s: In der Mitte der Brücke steht ein Turm.
sn.e: There is a tower in the middle of the bridge.
The tower stands in the water.
It is made of stone.
The tower is eight-sided.
It is called the Wasserturm.

sn.s: Der Turm ist älter als die Brücke.
sn.e: The tower is older than the bridge.

sn.s: Der Turm steht schon da, dann kommt die Brücke.
sn.e: The tower is standing there first, then the bridge comes.

sn.s: Das Feuer nimmt den Turm nicht.
sn.e: The fire does not take the tower.

sn.s: Ein Turm aus Stein brennt nicht.
sn.e: A tower made of stone does not burn.

sn.s: Genau wie das Tor am Bahnhof.
sn.e: Exactly like the gate at the station.
Stone stays, wood burns.
There are flowers along the railing.
The flowers are red.
They are red and white.
The whole bridge has flowers.

sn.s: Jemand giesst die Blumen jeden Tag.
sn.e: Somebody waters the flowers every day.

sn.s: Die Blumen hängen über dem Wasser.
sn.e: The flowers hang over the water.

sn.s: Von unten sieht das gut aus.
sn.e: From below it looks good.

sn.s: Ich gehe bis ans andere Ende.
sn.e: I walk to the other end.
Then I walk back again.

sn.s: Ich gehe viermal über die Brücke.
sn.e: I cross the bridge four times.
I do not have to be anywhere.

sn.s: Ich stehe in der Mitte und schaue.
sn.e: I stand in the middle and look.
To the left is the town.
To the right is the lake.
Up ahead stand the mountains.
Below me birds are swimming.
People walk past next to me.
Some of them look up.
Some do not look at all.

sn.s: Für sie ist die Brücke nur der Weg.
sn.e: For them the bridge is just the way across.
They walk here every day.

sn.s: Am Abend gehe ich noch einmal hin.
sn.e: In the evening I go there again.
The bridge has lights.
The wood looks warm.
The water is black.

sn.s: Der Turm steht dunkel im See.
sn.e: The tower stands dark in the lake.

sn.s: Ich schaue noch einmal nach oben.
sn.e: I look up once more.

sn.s: Im Licht sehe ich die Bilder besser.
sn.e: In the light I can see the pictures better.
Old pictures and new wood.
Both belong to it now.

lessons.title: Punkt acht
lessons.desc: Time, said exactly

sn.e: I have an appointment.

sn.s: Der Termin ist um acht Uhr.
sn.e: The appointment is at eight o'clock.

sn.s: Ein Termin ist hier ein Versprechen.
sn.e: An appointment here is a promise.
Eight o'clock sharp.
Sharp means: exactly then.
Not earlier and not later.
I look at the clock.
It is half past seven.

sn.s: Halb acht heisst: dreissig Minuten vor acht.
sn.e: Halb acht means: thirty minutes before eight.
That is hard at the start.

sn.s: Halb acht ist nicht acht Uhr dreissig.
sn.e: Halb acht is not eight thirty.

sn.s: Halb acht ist sieben Uhr dreissig.
sn.e: Halb acht is seven thirty.

sn.s: Man zählt zur nächsten Stunde hin.
sn.e: You count towards the next hour.

sn.s: Viertel vor acht ist sieben Uhr fünfundvierzig.
sn.e: Quarter to eight is seven forty-five.

sn.s: Viertel nach acht ist acht Uhr fünfzehn.
sn.e: Quarter past eight is eight fifteen.
A quarter is fifteen minutes.

sn.s: Eine halbe Stunde ist dreissig Minuten.
sn.e: Half an hour is thirty minutes.
I still have time.

sn.s: Ich habe eine halbe Stunde Zeit.
sn.e: I have half an hour.
That is enough time.
I have another coffee.

sn.s: Der Kaffee ist heiss und ich trinke langsam.
sn.e: The coffee is hot and I drink slowly.

sn.s: Ich schaue nicht auf die Uhr.
sn.e: I do not look at the clock.
That is a mistake.
Then I do look.
It is quarter to eight.
I am not late yet.
Late here really means late.

sn.s: Aber ich bin auch nicht früh.
sn.e: But I am not early either.
I stand up and go.
The walk takes ten minutes.
I need twelve.

sn.s: Ich finde die Strasse nicht sofort.
sn.e: I do not find the street right away.
Then I do find it.

sn.s: Ich komme um vier nach acht an.
sn.e: I arrive at four past eight.
Four minutes late.
Only four minutes.
At home that is nothing.
Here it is something.
Everybody else is already there.
They all come before eight.
They are sitting and waiting.
It starts at eight sharp.

sn.s: Es beginnt nicht um fünf nach acht.
sn.e: It does not begin at five past eight.
It really does start at eight sharp.
Only I am late.
I say sorry.
Sorry, I say again.
An apology costs nothing.
Entschuldigung is an important word.
I hear Entschuldigung a lot here.
A man nods.
Nobody says anything about it.
But everybody notices.
And I notice it too.

sn.s: Vier Minuten sind hier vier Minuten.
sn.e: Four minutes here are four minutes.
Time is exact.
It is exact everywhere.

sn.s: Der Zug fährt um zehn Uhr zwölf.
sn.e: The train leaves at ten twelve.
Not at ten thirteen.

sn.s: Der Bus kommt um sieben Uhr vier.
sn.e: The bus comes at four past seven.

sn.s: Und er kommt um sieben Uhr vier.
sn.e: And it comes at four past seven.

sn.s: Der Laden macht um halb sieben auf.
sn.e: The shop opens at half past six.
Exactly at half past six.

sn.s: Das ist kein Spruch über die Schweiz.
sn.e: That is not a saying about Switzerland.
That is simply the timetable.
Everybody keeps to it.

sn.s: Darum ist der Fahrplan ein Versprechen.
sn.e: That is why the timetable is a promise.

sn.s: Am nächsten Tag habe ich wieder einen Termin.
sn.e: The next day I have an appointment again.

sn.s: Der Termin ist um zwei Uhr.
sn.e: The appointment is at two o'clock.
This time I set off early.

sn.s: Ich bin um Viertel vor zwei da.
sn.e: I am there at quarter to two.
Fifteen minutes early.
Too early is odd as well.
I wait outside.

sn.s: Ich gehe um die Ecke und wieder zurück.
sn.e: I walk round the corner and back again.

sn.s: Um fünf vor zwei gehe ich hinein.
sn.e: At five to two I go in.

sn.s: Fünf Minuten früher ist genau richtig.
sn.e: Five minutes early is exactly right.
Not twenty and not zero.
It starts at two sharp.

sn.s: Alles beginnt genau dann, wenn es das sagt.
sn.e: Everything begins exactly when it says it will.
This time I am not a topic.
Nobody looks at me.
That is a good feeling.

sn.s: Am Abend stelle ich meine Uhr genau.
sn.e: In the evening I set my watch exactly.

sn.s: Ich stelle sie nach dem Bahnhof.
sn.e: I set it by the station clock.

sn.s: Die Uhr am Bahnhof ist gross und weiss.
sn.e: The clock at the station is big and white.
It has a red hand.

sn.s: Der rote Zeiger geht rund und hält kurz an.
sn.e: The red hand goes round and pauses briefly.
Then the minute jumps.

sn.s: Diese Uhr hängt in jedem Bahnhof.
sn.e: That clock hangs in every station.
The same clock everywhere.
The same time everywhere.

sn.s: Ich schaue oft auf die Uhr.
sn.e: I look at the clock a lot.
Soon I will look less.

sn.s: Bald weiss ich, wie spät es ist.
sn.e: Soon I will know what time it is.
And I will simply be there.
Eight o'clock sharp.

lessons.title: Am Sonntag ist zu
lessons.desc: The day everything stops

sn.e: It is Saturday.
Saturday is a good day.
The day goes past quickly.
The town is full.
All the shops are open.
On Saturday everybody does their shopping.
I do nothing.
I go to the lake.
I sit on the shore.
The day is beautiful.
In the evening I go back.

sn.s: Am Abend ist die Stadt ruhig.
sn.e: In the evening the town is quiet.

sn.s: Es ist halb sieben am Abend.
sn.e: It is half past six in the evening.
I need milk.
I have no milk left.
I go to the shop.
The shop is closed.
Geschlossen means: not open.
I look at the sign.
Saturday until five.

sn.s: Der Laden schliesst am Samstag früh.
sn.e: The shop closes early on Saturday.
It closes earlier than usual.
It closes at five.

sn.s: Ich bin anderthalb Stunden zu spät.
sn.e: I am an hour and a half too late.
I go to the other shop.

sn.s: Der andere Laden ist auch geschlossen.
sn.e: The other shop is closed too.
Both are shut.
Zu also means closed.

sn.s: Man sagt einfach: es ist zu.
sn.e: People just say: it is shut.
No problem, I think.
I will go tomorrow.
Tomorrow is Sunday.
On Sunday everything is shut.
Really everything.
On Sunday no shop opens.
The Migros does not open.
The Coop does not open either.

sn.s: Die Bäckerei öffnet manchmal am Morgen.
sn.e: The bakery sometimes opens in the morning.
But only briefly.

sn.s: Sonst ist der ganze Sonntag zu.
sn.e: Otherwise the whole of Sunday is shut.
I do not know that yet.

sn.s: Am Sonntag stehe ich auf und gehe zum Laden.
sn.e: On Sunday I get up and go to the shop.
The shop is closed.
I go to the next one.
Closed too.

sn.s: Ich gehe durch die halbe Stadt.
sn.e: I walk through half the town.
Everything is shut.
The streets are empty.

sn.s: Am Sonntag ist die Stadt ruhig.
sn.e: On Sunday the town is quiet.
Very quiet.
People go for walks.
Families go to the lake.

sn.s: Ein Mann liest auf einer Bank.
sn.e: A man is reading on a bench.
Nobody buys anything.
There is nothing to buy.

sn.s: Ich habe immer noch keine Milch.
sn.e: I still have no milk.

sn.s: Ich frage eine Frau auf der Strasse.
sn.e: I ask a woman in the street.
Grüezi, is anything open anywhere?
She says: at the station.

sn.s: Am Bahnhof sind die Läden offen.
sn.e: At the station the shops are open.
On Sunday too.
In the evening too.
The station is the exception.
Everybody here knows that.
Merci vielmal, I say.
I go to the station.
There is a shop in the station.
The shop is open.
It is small and expensive.
But it is open.
I buy milk.

sn.s: Die Milch kostet mehr als sonst.
sn.e: The milk costs more than usual.
I do not mind.
There are a lot of people in the shop.
Everybody forgets the same thing.
Milk, bread, a bit of cheese.

sn.s: Wir stehen alle am Sonntag am Bahnhof.
sn.e: We are all at the station on Sunday.
That is almost funny.

sn.s: Am Montag ist wieder alles offen.
sn.e: On Monday everything is open again.
The week starts.

sn.s: Eine Woche hat sechs Tage zum Einkaufen.
sn.e: A week has six days for shopping.

sn.s: Die ganze Woche ist alles offen.
sn.e: All week everything is open.

sn.s: Die Woche geht von Montag bis Samstag.
sn.e: The week runs from Monday to Saturday.
On Sunday the week rests.

sn.s: Jetzt kaufe ich am Freitag ein.
sn.e: Now I do my shopping on Friday.
Or on Saturday morning.
Never on Saturday evening.

sn.s: Ich schaue jetzt auf die Schilder.
sn.e: Now I look at the signs.

sn.s: Auf jedem Laden stehen die Zeiten.
sn.e: Every shop has its hours on the door.

sn.s: Wann er öffnet und wann er schliesst.
sn.e: When it opens and when it closes.
Everybody here closes on time.
I read it beforehand.

sn.s: Der Sonntag ist jetzt kein Problem.
sn.e: Sunday is not a problem now.
Sunday is actually nice.
A day with no appointments.
A day without shops.

sn.s: Man geht an den See und das ist alles.
sn.e: You go to the lake and that is that.

sn.s: Man braucht nur Milch am Samstag.
sn.e: You just need milk on Saturday.

lessons.title: Es regnet
lessons.desc: Weather you will talk about every day

sn.e: It is raining.
It has been raining since morning.
It is raining quietly.
The rain is not heavy.

sn.s: Aber der Regen hört nicht auf.
sn.e: But the rain does not stop.
I go to the bakery.
I do not have an umbrella.
I get wet.
My jacket is wet.
My shoes are wet too.
Wet is not a good feeling.

sn.s: In der Bäckerei sagt die Frau Grüezi.
sn.e: In the bakery the woman says Grüezi.

sn.s: Dann sagt sie: heute regnet es.
sn.e: Then she says: it is raining today.
Yes, I say. It is raining.

sn.s: Das ist mein erstes Gespräch über das Wetter.
sn.e: That is my first conversation about the weather.
It is not the last.
Outside I meet a neighbour.
He says: rain again.
Yes, I say.

sn.s: Im Laden sagt ein Mann: was für ein Wetter.
sn.e: In the shop a man says: what weather.

sn.s: Drei Leute reden vor zehn Uhr über das Wetter.
sn.e: Three people talk about the weather before ten.

sn.s: Das Wetter ist immer ein Thema.
sn.e: The weather is always a topic.
You start with it.
It is not empty chatter.
It is simply the opening.
It rains a lot in Luzern.

sn.s: Es regnet mehr als in Zürich.
sn.e: It rains more than in Zurich.
Everybody here says so.
They almost say it with pleasure.

sn.s: Der Berg holt den Regen, sagt jemand.
sn.e: The mountain pulls in the rain, somebody says.
Pilatus stands in the way.

sn.s: Der Pilatus hat einen Hut, dann kommt Regen.
sn.e: Pilatus has a hat on, then rain comes.

sn.s: Ein Hut ist eine Wolke oben auf dem Berg.
sn.e: A hat is a cloud on top of the mountain.

sn.s: Ich schaue jetzt immer zum Berg.
sn.e: Now I always look at the mountain.
I buy an umbrella.

sn.s: Der Schirm ist klein und schwarz.
sn.e: The umbrella is small and black.

sn.s: Der Schirm ist im Sack, immer.
sn.e: The umbrella is in my bag, always.

sn.s: Man hat hier einen Schirm dabei.
sn.e: Here you carry an umbrella.
Even in sunshine.

sn.s: Dann kommt ein Tag ohne Regen.
sn.e: Then a day comes with no rain.
It is warm.
Warm and dry in October.

sn.s: Es ist sehr warm für die Jahreszeit.
sn.e: It is very warm for the time of year.

sn.s: Die Luft ist warm und trocken.
sn.e: The air is warm and dry.
The sky is very clear.
The mountains look close.

sn.s: Sie sehen viel näher aus als sonst.
sn.e: They look much closer than usual.
You can see every stone.

sn.s: Das ist der Föhn, sagt die Frau in der Bäckerei.
sn.e: That is the Föhn, the woman in the bakery says.
The Föhn is a wind.
The wind comes suddenly.

sn.s: Der Wind kommt über die Berge.
sn.e: The wind comes over the mountains.
It comes from the south.

sn.s: Der Wind ist warm und trocken.
sn.e: The wind is warm and dry.

sn.s: Ein warmer Wind im Oktober ist komisch.
sn.e: A warm wind in October is odd.

sn.s: Beim Föhn ist die Luft anders.
sn.e: During the Föhn the air is different.
Everything is sharp and close.

sn.s: Der Föhn ist schön und alle klagen.
sn.e: The Föhn is beautiful and everybody complains.

sn.s: Der Kopf tut weh, sagen sie.
sn.e: My head hurts, they say.

sn.s: Ich kann nicht schlafen, sagen sie.
sn.e: I cannot sleep, they say.

sn.s: Die Kinder sind wild, sagen sie.
sn.e: The children are wild, they say.
Everything is the Föhn.

sn.s: Der Föhn ist an allem schuld.
sn.e: The Föhn is to blame for everything.

sn.s: Nach dem Föhn kommt oft Regen.
sn.e: After the Föhn rain often comes.
And the rain does come.

sn.s: Am nächsten Tag regnet es wieder.
sn.e: The next day it rains again.

sn.s: Diesmal habe ich den Schirm dabei.
sn.e: This time I have the umbrella with me.
I do not get wet.
That is a small victory.
In October it gets cold.
The rain gets cold.

sn.s: Kalter Regen ist schlimmer als viel Regen.
sn.e: Cold rain is worse than a lot of rain.

sn.s: Oben auf den Bergen liegt Schnee.
sn.e: There is snow on the mountains.
The snow stays up there.
The snow comes lower down.

sn.s: Jede Woche kommt der Schnee tiefer.
sn.e: Every week the snow comes lower.
Down here it is not snowing yet.
A little later it does snow.

sn.s: In der Stadt schneit es selten.
sn.e: In town it rarely snows.

sn.s: Am See bleibt der Schnee nicht liegen.
sn.e: By the lake the snow does not settle.

sn.s: Oben schneit es die ganze Woche.
sn.e: Up there it snows all week.

sn.s: Ein Mann sagt: bald schneit es auch hier.
sn.e: A man says: soon it will snow down here too.

sn.s: Er sagt es wie eine Warnung.
sn.e: He says it like a warning.
And like something good.

sn.s: Ich schaue jeden Morgen aus dem Fenster.
sn.e: I look out of the window every morning.
Rain or no rain.

sn.s: Wolke auf dem Berg oder nicht.
sn.e: Cloud on the mountain or not.
Then I know the weather.

sn.s: Und ich habe einen Satz für die Bäckerei.
sn.e: And I have a sentence for the bakery.
Grüezi. It is raining again today.
That is not much.
But it is something.

lessons.title: Die erste Nacht
lessons.desc: A room, a window, and a great deal of quiet

sn.e: I have a room.
The room is small.
It is small and clean.
There is a bed in the room.

sn.s: Das Bett steht an der Wand.
sn.e: The bed stands against the wall.

sn.s: Neben dem Bett steht ein Tisch.
sn.e: There is a table next to the bed.

sn.s: Auf dem Tisch liegt mein Geld.
sn.e: My money is lying on the table.
Notes and coins.
Next to it lies my ticket.

sn.s: Das Billett von Zürich nach Luzern.
sn.e: The ticket from Zurich to Luzern.
I am keeping it.
There is a window in the room.
The window is big.

sn.s: Aus dem Fenster sehe ich ein Dach.
sn.e: Out of the window I see a roof.

sn.s: Über dem Dach sehe ich den Berg.
sn.e: Above the roof I see the mountain.
The mountain is dark.

sn.s: Der Koffer steht noch am Boden.
sn.e: The suitcase is still on the floor.

sn.s: Er ist noch nicht ganz leer.
sn.e: It is not completely empty yet.
I am tired.
I am very tired.
The day is long.
I lie down in the bed.
The bed is good.

sn.s: Ich liege und schaue an die Decke.
sn.e: I lie there and look at the ceiling.

sn.s: Ich bin müde und ich schlafe nicht.
sn.e: I am tired and I am not sleeping.
I cannot sleep.
Sleeping simply does not work today.
It is ten o'clock.
Ten o’clock is late here.
At ten it goes quiet.

sn.s: Um zehn hört man nichts mehr.
sn.e: At ten you hear nothing more.
The town goes suddenly quiet.
Before that I hear people.
After ten I hear nothing.
I really do hear nothing.
No cars.
No people in the street.
No music.
After ten there is quiet.

sn.s: In der Nacht fährt kein Bus mehr.
sn.e: At night no bus runs any more.
That is a rule here.
Everybody keeps to it.

sn.s: Ich liege und höre der Stille zu.
sn.e: I lie there and listen to the silence.
The silence is loud.

sn.s: Keine Nacht zu Hause ist so laut.
sn.e: No night at home is this loud.

sn.s: Ich höre die Uhr an der Wand.
sn.e: I hear the clock on the wall.

sn.s: Ich höre das Wasser in der Leitung.
sn.e: I hear the water in the pipe.
Once I hear a train.
The train is far away.
Then it is quiet again.
I am alone.

sn.s: Allein im Zimmer ist es sehr still.
sn.e: Alone in the room it is very quiet.
I am completely alone here.
I do not know anybody.

sn.s: Ich kenne Lea vom Café ein bisschen.
sn.e: I know Lea from the café a little.

sn.s: Und die Frau von der Bäckerei.
sn.e: And the woman from the bakery.
That is all.
Two people in two weeks.

sn.s: Allein sein ist nicht immer schlimm.
sn.e: Being alone is not always bad.

sn.s: Heute bin ich lieber nicht allein.
sn.e: Today I would rather not be alone.

sn.s: Heute ist es ein bisschen schlimm.
sn.e: Today it is a little bad.

sn.s: Ich denke an den ersten Tag.
sn.e: I think about the first day.

sn.s: Der Flughafen und die vierzig Minuten.
sn.e: The airport and the forty minutes.
The first word.

sn.s: Das erste Mal ist immer das schwerste.
sn.e: The first time is always the hardest.
Grüezi.
Back then it is hard.

sn.s: Heute sage ich es einfach so.
sn.e: Today I just say it.

sn.s: Ich sage es zehnmal am Tag.
sn.e: I say it ten times a day.

sn.s: Ich denke an das Gleis sieben.
sn.e: I think about track seven.
And the ninety seconds.

sn.s: Ich denke an den Brunnen und das Wasser.
sn.e: I think about the fountain and the water.

sn.s: Ich denke an die fünfzig Franken für einen Kaffee.
sn.e: I think about the fifty francs for one coffee.

sn.s: Ich denke an den Mann von der Post.
sn.e: I think about the man from the post office.

sn.s: Er geht den ganzen Weg wieder zurück.
sn.e: He walks the whole way back again.

sn.s: Ich denke an die Brücke aus Holz.
sn.e: I think about the wooden bridge.

sn.s: Und an den See und die Berge dahinter.
sn.e: And the lake and the mountains behind it.
Two weeks is not long.
But it is something.
I can order a coffee.
I can buy a Gipfeli.

sn.s: Ich kann nach dem Weg fragen.
sn.e: I can ask the way.
I can read the clock.

sn.s: Ich weiss die Zeiten von den Läden.
sn.e: I know the shop hours.

sn.s: Am Sonntag ist alles zu, und ich weiss es.
sn.e: On Sunday everything is shut, and I know it.
That is not much German.

sn.s: Aber es ist genug für einen Tag.
sn.e: But it is enough for one day.
Tomorrow is another day.
Tomorrow I will look for a flat.
A room is not a home.
A flat maybe is.

sn.s: Ich liege im Bett und bin müde.
sn.e: I lie in bed and I am tired.
I have been tired for a long time.
Next door somebody is already asleep.
Outside it is quiet.
The mountain stands at the window.
At some point I fall asleep.

sn.s: Ich schlafe schlecht und ich schlafe doch.
sn.e: I sleep badly and I sleep all the same.

sn.s: Die erste Nacht ist die längste.
sn.e: The first night is the longest.

sn.s: Die Nacht ist lang und still.
sn.e: The night is long and quiet.

sn.s: Es ist meine erste Nacht in dieser Wohnung.
sn.e: It is my first night in this flat.
The second is shorter.

lessons.title: Die Wohnung
lessons.desc: Three keys, and what each one is for

sn.e: I have a flat.
The flat is small.

sn.s: Sie hat zwei Zimmer, eine Küche und ein Bad.
sn.e: It has two rooms, a kitchen and a bathroom.

sn.s: Die Wohnung ist im dritten Stock.
sn.e: The flat is on the third floor.

sn.s: Der Stock ist hier nicht das Erdgeschoss.
sn.e: The floor here is not the ground floor.
The ground floor is zero.

sn.s: Der erste Stock ist der zweite Stock von unten.
sn.e: The first floor is the second one up.

sn.s: Ein Stock mehr ist eine Treppe mehr.
sn.e: One floor more is one flight more.

sn.s: Ich muss das jedes Mal neu denken.
sn.e: I have to work that out again every time.
The landlord is called Herr Kaufmann.
He comes at two o'clock.
He comes at two o'clock sharp.

sn.s: Er hat drei Schlüssel in der Hand.
sn.e: He has three keys in his hand.
He gives me the keys.

sn.s: Der erste Schlüssel ist für die Wohnung.
sn.e: The first key is for the flat.

sn.s: Der zweite Schlüssel ist für das Haus.
sn.e: The second key is for the building.

sn.s: Der dritte Schlüssel ist für den Keller.
sn.e: The third key is for the cellar.
The cellar is downstairs.

sn.s: Im Keller habe ich ein Abteil.
sn.e: In the cellar I have a compartment.
The compartment is empty.

sn.s: Ich brauche den Keller noch nicht.
sn.e: I do not need the cellar yet.

sn.s: Herr Kaufmann sagt alles noch einmal.
sn.e: Herr Kaufmann says everything again.

sn.s: Der erste Schlüssel für die Wohnung.
sn.e: The first key for the flat.
The second for the building.
The third for the cellar.

sn.s: Ich verstehe es beim ersten Mal.
sn.e: I understand it the first time.
He says it twice anyway.

sn.s: Dann zeigt er mir die Küche.
sn.e: Then he shows me the kitchen.

sn.s: Die Küche ist klein und sehr sauber.
sn.e: The kitchen is small and very clean.

sn.s: In der Küche gibt es einen Herd.
sn.e: In the kitchen there is a cooker.
There is a fridge too.

sn.s: Der Kühlschrank ist leer und offen.
sn.e: The fridge is empty and open.

sn.s: Der Kühlschrank ist klein und alt.
sn.e: The fridge is small and old.
A fridge belongs to the flat.

sn.s: Er muss offen sein, sagt Herr Kaufmann.
sn.e: It has to stay open, says Herr Kaufmann.
Otherwise it smells.

sn.s: In der Küche darf man nicht rauchen.
sn.e: In the kitchen you may not smoke.

sn.s: In der ganzen Wohnung darf man nicht rauchen.
sn.e: In the whole flat you may not smoke.

sn.s: Rauchen ist im ganzen Haus verboten.
sn.e: Smoking is forbidden in the whole building.

sn.s: Im Treppenhaus darf auch niemand rauchen.
sn.e: Nobody may smoke in the stairwell either.
I do not smoke.
Good, he says.

sn.s: Dann zeigt er mir das Bad.
sn.e: Then he shows me the bathroom.
The bathroom is very small.
There is a window in the bathroom.
You have to open the window.

sn.s: Nach dem Duschen macht man das Fenster auf.
sn.e: After showering you open the window.
Otherwise you get mould.
Mould is expensive, he says.
I do not write that down.
But I remember it.
The flat is completely white.

sn.s: Die Wände sind weiss und leer.
sn.e: The walls are white and empty.
The floor is wood.
The floor is very clean.
Everything is clean.
The flat is too clean.

sn.s: Meine alte Wohnung ist nie so sauber.
sn.e: My old flat is never this clean.
Herr Kaufmann sees my face.
He explains it to me.
You get a flat clean.

sn.s: Und man gibt sie sauber zurück.
sn.e: And you give it back clean.

sn.s: Am Ende kommt jemand und schaut alles an.
sn.e: At the end somebody comes and looks at everything.
That is called the handover.

sn.s: Bei der Wohnungsabgabe schaut man in jede Ecke.
sn.e: At the handover they look in every corner.

sn.s: Man schaut auch hinter den Herd.
sn.e: They look behind the cooker too.
And in the fridge.

sn.s: Man muss die Wohnung sehr gut putzen.
sn.e: You have to clean the flat very well.
A lot of people do not clean it themselves.
They pay somebody.
Cleaning then costs five hundred francs.

sn.s: Fünfhundert Franken nur für das Putzen.
sn.e: Five hundred francs just for the cleaning.

sn.s: Ich kann selber putzen, sage ich.
sn.e: I can clean it myself, I say.
He laughs briefly.

sn.s: Das sagen alle am Anfang, sagt er.
sn.e: Everybody says that at the start, he says.

sn.s: Dann gibt er mir ein Papier.
sn.e: Then he gives me a piece of paper.

sn.s: Auf dem Papier steht die Miete.
sn.e: The rent is on the paper.
The rent is twelve hundred francs.

sn.s: Die Miete muss ich jeden Monat bezahlen.
sn.e: I have to pay the rent every month.

sn.s: Die Miete ist mein grösster Betrag.
sn.e: The rent is my biggest outgoing.

sn.s: Ich muss sie bis am dritten bezahlen.
sn.e: I have to pay it by the third.
Not on the fourth, he says.
The rent is a lot of money.
But the flat is good.

sn.s: Und sie ist nah am Bahnhof.
sn.e: And it is close to the station.
Then Herr Kaufmann leaves.

sn.s: Er sagt: Sie können mich immer anrufen.
sn.e: He says: you can always ring me.

sn.s: Aber rufen Sie den Hauswart an.
sn.e: But ring the caretaker.
The caretaker does most of it.

sn.s: Er sagt Ade und geht die Treppe hinunter.
sn.e: He says Ade and goes down the stairs.

sn.s: Ich bin allein in der Wohnung.
sn.e: I am alone in the flat.
I stand in the kitchen.

sn.s: Ich habe drei Schlüssel in der Hand.
sn.e: I have three keys in my hand.

sn.s: Ich lege die Schlüssel auf den Tisch.
sn.e: I put the keys on the table.
There is no table.

sn.s: Ich lege sie auf den Boden.
sn.e: I put them on the floor.
I have no furniture.

sn.s: Ich habe einen Koffer und drei Schlüssel.
sn.e: I have one suitcase and three keys.
I walk through the flat.
Room, room, kitchen, bathroom.
Then again.
I open every window.
The air is cold.

sn.s: Aus dem Fenster sehe ich den Berg.
sn.e: Out of the window I see the mountain.
I have to buy a lot.

sn.s: Ein Bett, einen Tisch, einen Stuhl.
sn.e: A bed, a table, a chair.
I can do that tomorrow.
Today I am doing nothing more.

sn.s: Ich setze mich auf den Boden.
sn.e: I sit down on the floor.
